summary: A comment from BBN that the Terminal IMP cannot directly use the proposed mailbox protocol. It cannot store incoming messages for later printing, is not expected to act as a server, and cannot run programs to process varied input. Another host would have to do those jobs for terminals attached to it.

plainLanguage.summary: BBN explains why a Terminal IMP cannot directly provide mailboxes: it cannot store messages or run the needed server programs. A larger host could store messages for Terminal IMP users to read later.

questions: why terminal imp could not use mailbox protocol
why could a terminal imp not host mailboxes
subtitle: Why a Terminal IMP needed a remote host to store and serve mail.

tldr.problem: The Terminal IMP could not store incoming messages, act as a server or process varied input streams, so it could not directly implement the proposed mailbox protocol.
tldr.mechanism: BBN suggests allowing Terminal IMP users to rent mailboxes on a larger host and retrieve messages through Telnet.
tldr.outcome: The remote mailbox approach avoids requiring a dedicated printer at each Terminal IMP site.

today: RFC 224 is a comment on the mailbox protocol published in September 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Terminal IMP Limitations
sections.content:
BBN lists three limits that prevent a Terminal IMP from directly implementing the proposed mailbox protocol. It cannot store incoming messages for later printing or display, is not expected to act as a server, and cannot run programs to process different input streams.

It supports Telnet and might support a mode of the Data Transfer Protocol, but was not expected to support the File Transfer Protocol or transform data such as line-printer controls or character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: The Terminal IMP can connect a terminal to network services, but it cannot keep messages or run the server-side programs needed for a mailbox.

sections.title: Renting Mailbox Storage
sections.content:
BBN proposes that Terminal IMP installations be allowed to rent mailboxes at a larger host, with the NIC suggested as a possible location. Messages for Terminal IMP users would be sent to that host and stored there.

A user could periodically log in to the host with Telnet to examine the mailbox. The host would handle any needed data transformation before sending the message to the Terminal IMP.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger host stores the messages for Terminal IMP users. Users can connect later and read them through Telnet.

sections.title: Dedicated Printer Alternative
sections.content:
The RFC considers a dedicated mailbox printer at each Terminal IMP site. The authors say a Terminal IMP could then accept mail from only one sender at a time, and the printer would limit transmission speed.

They also note that one central printer could serve poorly when terminals are spread across a wide area. BBN considers remote mailbox storage more cost-effective than a special printer at every site.
sections.plainLanguage: A local printer would limit mail to one sender at a time and to printer speed. The authors prefer storing mail at a larger host.
